**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

---

**The Korean War: the world you were born into**

When you arrived on February 20, 1952, American soldiers had been dying in Korea for nineteen months. The war had pivoted from dramatic mobile warfare — the Inchon landing, the Chinese intervention, the catastrophic retreat from the Chosin Reservoir — to a grinding, frozen stalemate near the 38th parallel that neither side could break. Armistice negotiations had been underway at Panmunjom since July 1951, but talks had stalled bitterly over the question of prisoner repatriation. They would drag on for another seventeen months after you were born, finally concluding in July 1953.

The Korean War is sometimes called the Forgotten War — overshadowed by the Second World War that preceded it and the Vietnam War that followed. But in February 1952, it was not forgotten. It was immediate. The United States was at war the week you were born, in a conflict that ended without a peace treaty and whose ceasefire line remains, in 2026, the most heavily militarized border on Earth.

---

**The Oslo Winter Olympics — in progress on your birthday**

The VI Winter Olympics were underway in Oslo, Norway (February 14–25, 1952), meaning the Games were live on the day you were born. Hjalmar Andersen of Norway dominated the speed skating events, winning three gold medals before his home crowd. The Games were still largely a radio-and-newsreel event in most of the world — television coverage of the Winter Olympics was years away. The contrast between Oslo's peaceful winter competition and the frozen combat in Korea was not lost on observers at the time.

---

**Your tenth birthday: John Glenn orbits Earth**

On February 20, 1962 — the exact date of your tenth birthday — Marine pilot and astronaut John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, completing three circuits aboard *Friendship 7* before splashing down in the Atlantic. The nation watched on television. The timing is not metaphor; it is simply true: on the morning you turned ten, a human being was circling the planet above you. Glenn's flight came ten months after Yuri Gagarin's orbital mission had alarmed the American public, and it partially restored national confidence in the Space Race. It remains one of the most exact-date coincidences available to anyone born in 1952.

---

**The worst polio year in American history**

1952 would prove to be the most devastating year of the American polio epidemic — 57,628 cases were reported, more than any year before or since. In the summer of 1952, parents kept children away from swimming pools and crowded places. Iron lungs filled hospital wards. Jonas Salk, working at the University of Pittsburgh, was in the middle of developing the vaccine that would end the epidemic — but it would not be announced safe and effective until April 1955, three years after your birth. You were born in the worst year of a disease that paralyzed thousands of children annually, in the years just before it was stopped. The Salk vaccine is one of the signal medical achievements of the 20th century, and its development ran almost exactly parallel to your first three years of life.

---

**±30 days: A new queen**

Fourteen days before your birth, on February 6, 1952, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. Princess Elizabeth, 25 years old and on safari in Kenya with her husband, learned the news and flew home as Queen Elizabeth II. Her coronation the following June became one of the first major shared global television events — an estimated 20 million people in Britain alone watched, many on sets borrowed or seen at neighbors' homes for the occasion. Elizabeth II would reign for 70 years, dying in September 2022. She outlasted the Korean War, the Cold War, the British Empire's dissolution, and most of the institutions that defined the world she inherited. Her reign began two weeks before you drew your first breath and extended well into your seventh decade.

---

**The arc of 74 years**

You were born in the middle of an undeclared war, the worst year of a child-paralyzing epidemic, and the early months of a decade that would test nearly every assumption the postwar world had made about stability, progress, and what America was for.

In 74 years: polio was eradicated in most of the world. The Korean armistice held, imperfectly. Television absorbed politics, culture, and daily life. Humans reached the Moon. Vietnam began and ended. Watergate. The fall of the Berlin Wall. The Soviet Union dissolved. The internet arrived. The smartphone. Now AI.

You were born when the primary experience of the world beyond your street was radio, newspaper, and word of mouth. You inhabit 2026, when the sum of recorded human knowledge is searchable in seconds on a device in your pocket. The distance between those two sentences is your life.
